name: Droperidol
summary: Short-acting injectable antipsychotic/antiemetic used in the OR and emergency department, mainly for acute agitation and rescue treatment of nausea/vomiting. Powerful but carries a boxed warning for heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation and torsades).
description: Droperidol is an older antipsychotic that most people meet in the operating room or emergency department. At low doses it helps with nausea and vomiting. At higher doses it can rapidly calm severe agitation. Because it can prolong the heart’s QT interval and trigger dangerous arrhythmias, it’s reserved for situations where safer options have not worked and ECG monitoring is available.
patient_summary: Droperidol is an injectable medication used in hospitals to quickly calm severe agitation or treat bad nausea and vomiting, usually after surgery. It works fast—often within minutes—but it can affect your heart rhythm, so it’s typically given only when other options haven’t helped and while you’re on a heart monitor.

primary_indications: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) – prevention and rescue
Acute undifferentiated agitation in emergency settings (off-label)

linked_conditions.context: Used IM or IV for rapid sedation in severely agitated patients when other options (benzodiazepines, other antipsychotics) are ineffective or not tolerated.
Labeled for prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting related to surgery and diagnostic procedures, typically at low IV doses.
Sometimes considered when delirium presents with dangerous agitation, but QT risk and EPS limit its role. Not a first-line delirium treatment.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to droperidol or formulation components
Known or suspected QT prolongation (including congenital long QT syndrome)
Baseline QTc >440 msec in males or >450 msec in females
History of torsades de pointes or serious ventricular arrhythmias
Bradycardia <50 bpm or clinically significant cardiac disease without monitoring
Concomitant use of other high-risk QT-prolonging drugs when monitoring is not available

efficacy_response.metric: Onset of calming for acute agitation
efficacy_response.percentage_value: Most patients show clinically meaningful calming within 10–30 minutes at typical doses
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Comparable to other injectable antipsychotics and benzodiazepine-based protocols in many emergency department protocols.
efficacy_response.patient_text: In real-world emergency department use, droperidol is valued because it usually starts taking the edge off agitation within minutes and can be repeated in small doses to get you calm but still breathing safely.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Clinical practice data; no single landmark trial defines efficacy.

pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: 2–4 hours of main clinical effect (sedation and antiemesis), with some patients experiencing effects up to 12 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic metabolism to multiple metabolites including p-fluorophenylacetic acid, benzimidazolone, and p-hydroxypiperidine
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily in urine (~75%, less than 1% unchanged) and feces (~22%)

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Droperidol is an injectable antipsychotic/antiemetic that shows up mostly in operating rooms and emergency departments. From a psychiatry lens, its main role is rapid control of severe agitation when other options have failed or are not tolerated. At much lower doses, it can also be used to treat nausea and vomiting around surgery.
items: Acute undifferentiated agitation: Rapid tranquilization in emergency settings, IM or IV, often alongside benzodiazepines.
Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV): Low-dose IV at the end of procedures to prevent or rescue nausea/vomiting.
Rescue when first-line options fail: Considered when more commonly used agents (ondansetron, haloperidol, benzodiazepines) are ineffective or poorly tolerated.
off_label: Severe behavioral disturbance associated with delirium (with careful ECG monitoring and only when safer options are not available).
Adjunctive sedation for painful or anxiety-provoking procedures in the ED or ICU when standard sedatives are insufficient.

sections.heading: What People Commonly Feel
sections.intro: Most people meet droperidol in a crisis—either very agitated or very nauseated. You’re usually already in the hospital, attached to monitors, and being watched closely.

quotes: I went from pacing and yelling to sitting quietly in the chair within about 10 minutes.
My body finally stopped fighting everything. I could feel myself letting go of the panic.
It didn’t knock me out completely, but it turned the volume way down on the agitation.
I felt like someone put a weighted blanket on my whole body.
Keeping my eyes open took effort—I mostly drifted in and out of sleep.
I was calm but also groggy and slow for a couple of hours.
My legs felt restless, like I had to keep moving even though I was tired.
My neck felt tight and uncomfortable, almost like it wanted to twist.
I felt jittery on the inside but looked calm from the outside.
items.note: These can be extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)—movement side effects that sometimes need treatment with medications like benztropine or diphenhydramine.

quotes: They kept me on a heart monitor the whole time and checked my EKG after.
The team talked a lot about my ‘QT’ and electrolytes before giving it.
It was reassuring but also a little scary to hear them talk about my heart rhythm.
items.note: Because droperidol can prolong the QT interval and trigger dangerous heart rhythms, ECG and vital sign monitoring are standard.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
sections.text: Droperidol is designed to work quickly and then wear off over a few hours, which is exactly what you want in an emergency or perioperative setting.
key_points: Onset: 3–10 minutes after IM or IV injection.
Peak effect: Around 30 minutes for sedation and antiemetic benefit.
Duration: Main effects typically last 2–4 hours, but some patients feel sedated for up to 12 hours.
Heart effects: QT prolongation risk overlaps with the first few hours after dosing, which is why ECG monitoring is continued for 2–3 hours after administration.
No daily pill: Droperidol is almost always used as one-time or short-course injectable dosing—not a maintenance home medication.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Time to calming for acute agitation
sections.comparison: Similar to other injectable antipsychotics and some benzo-based protocols used in emergency settings.
sections.text: In practice, droperidol is chosen for situations where clinicians need a reliable, injectable option that works quickly. When used for acute agitation, most patients show noticeable calming within the first 10–30 minutes, especially when combined thoughtfully with a benzodiazepine. For postoperative nausea and vomiting, low doses can reduce nausea and the need for additional rescue medications, but QT concerns have pushed many centers toward newer antiemetics as first-line.
sections.clinical_details: Droperidol’s modern role has been shaped more by emergency department and perioperative experience than by a single landmark trial. Common emergency department protocols using 5–10 mg IM or 2.5–10 mg IV, with repeat dosing up to 20 mg per episode, report reliable calming with acceptable respiratory safety when patients are properly monitored. For PONV, low doses around 0.625–1.25 mg IV at the end of surgery have been effective, though concerns about QT prolongation have limited first-line use.

citation.authors: Multiple perioperative and emergency medicine studies
citation.title: Clinical use of droperidol for acute agitation and postoperative nausea and vomiting

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Droperidol can prolong the QT interval and trigger torsade de pointes, a life-threatening heart rhythm. Use only when other reasonable options have failed and always with ECG monitoring.
sections.black_box: Cases of QT prolongation and torsade de pointes, including fatal events, have occurred at or below recommended doses, sometimes in patients without obvious risk factors. Obtain a baseline ECG and do NOT use droperidol if QTc is >440 ms in men or >450 ms in women. Monitor ECG and vital signs for 2–3 hours after dosing.
other: Contraindicated in known or suspected QT prolongation, including congenital long QT syndrome.
Use extreme caution in patients with heart failure, bradycardia, structural heart disease, or electrolyte disturbances (low potassium or magnesium).
Risk increases when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs or medications that lower potassium/magnesium (eg, diuretics).
May cause extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) such as dystonia, akathisia, and Parkinson-like stiffness.
Can cause significant sedation, low blood pressure, and impaired coordination, especially at higher or repeated doses.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a rare but life-threatening reaction, has been reported with antipsychotics including droperidol.
patient_counseling: Expect to be on a heart monitor before and after droperidol—this is for safety, not because something has already gone wrong.
Tell your team if you have a history of long QT, fainting spells, unexplained seizures, or sudden cardiac death in the family.
Let your clinicians know about any water pills (diuretics), heart medications, or other drugs that affect your heart rhythm.
Report any chest pounding, rapid or irregular heartbeat, dizziness, or feeling like you might faint immediately.
Tell staff right away if you feel extreme restlessness, muscle stiffness, twisting of the neck or eyes, or inner jitteriness—these may be treatable EPS.
Avoid driving, climbing stairs without support, or making big decisions until the sedating and cognitive effects have clearly worn off.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most concerning are heart rhythm problems (QT prolongation and torsades) and movement side effects (EPS). Sedation, dizziness, and blood-pressure drops are also common, especially at higher or repeated doses.
plain_language_list: Low blood pressure or feeling faint when standing
Restlessness, inner jitteriness, or muscle stiffness (EPS)
Mood changes (anxiety, low mood, or dysphoria)
Rare but serious heart rhythm changes, including torsades de pointes
Rare severe reactions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, confusion)

common.incidence: Common; more likely at higher doses or in combination with other sedatives
common.patient_note: You may feel very sleepy or groggy for several hours after an injection. This is partly intentional when treating agitation but can linger even after you feel calm. Staff should help you with walking or transfers to prevent falls.

common.incidence: Common; especially in older adults or those with dehydration or cardiovascular disease
common.patient_note: Standing up quickly may make you feel light-headed or like you might black out. Move slowly, ask for help when getting out of bed, and let staff know if you feel woozy or faint.

common.incidence: Uncommon at low antiemetic doses; more common at higher antipsychotic-range doses or in children and young adults
common.patient_note: EPS can feel like inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle stiffness, jaw or neck tightness, or eyes pulling upward. These reactions are uncomfortable but usually treatable with other medications if caught early.

Some people feel emotionally flat or mildly depressed after dosing; others feel briefly more anxious or uncomfortable. Let your team know if your mood feels significantly worse after receiving droperidol.
You may notice shaking or feeling chilled. Warm blankets and time usually help, but persistent or severe shivering should be reported.

serious: QT prolongation and torsade de pointes: Can present with palpitations, dizziness, fainting, or sudden collapse. This is a medical emergency.
Ventricular tachycardia or other severe arrhythmias: May cause sudden loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest.
Severe hypotension: Marked blood-pressure drop requiring fluids, positioning, or vasopressors.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): High fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure or heart rate. Requires immediate discontinuation and emergency treatment.
Laryngospasm, bronchospasm, or respiratory depression: Difficulty breathing, wheezing, or slowed respirations, especially when combined with opioids or benzodiazepines.
Tardive dyskinesia with prolonged or repeated antipsychotic exposure: Involuntary facial or limb movements that may be persistent.
Anaphylaxis: Very rare but serious allergic reaction with hives, swelling, or trouble breathing.

sections.heading: Drug Interactions
sections.intro: With droperidol, the big interaction themes are QT prolongation, electrolyte shifts, and stacking sedatives.

items.with: Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class I and III antiarrhythmics, some antipsychotics, certain SSRIs, macrolide antibiotics, fluoroquinolones)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation and increased risk of torsades de pointes or other ventricular arrhythmias.
items.action: Avoid combination when possible. If no alternatives, correct electrolytes, obtain baseline ECG, and monitor continuously.

items.risk: Low potassium or magnesium increases risk of QT prolongation and torsades.
items.action: Check and correct electrolytes before dosing. Use caution in patients on loop or thiazide diuretics or with vomiting/diarrhea.

items.with: Benzodiazepines, opioids, volatile anesthetics, and other CNS depressants
items.risk: Additive sedation, respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and falls.
items.action: These combos are common in the OR/ED but require careful dose selection, slow titration, and close monitoring of breathing and blood pressure.

items.with: Other antipsychotics and dopamine-blocking agents (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
items.risk: Increased risk of EPS, NMS, and QT prolongation.
items.action: Avoid stacking multiple dopamine blockers when possible; if needed, keep doses low and duration brief, and monitor closely for movement side effects.

items.risk: Potential additive CNS effects, blood-pressure changes, and QT interactions.
items.action: Use only if clearly necessary with careful monitoring. Consider non-QT-prolonging alternatives first.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Droperidol is usually given as a one-time or very short-term injection in the OR or emergency department, not as a daily home medication. That means classic tapering plans (like we use for SSRIs or benzodiazepines) generally do not apply.
key_points: No physiologic dependence pattern like benzodiazepines or opioids has been described with brief droperidol use.
Most patients receive only one or a few doses during a procedure or acute agitation episode, so there is usually nothing to taper.

If droperidol were ever used repeatedly as an antipsychotic (rare in modern practice), it would be reasonable to reduce the dose gradually over days to weeks to watch for symptom return or withdrawal dyskinesias.
After using droperidol for agitation, the real work is figuring out and treating the underlying condition—mood or psychotic disorders, substance use, delirium, or medical illness.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: All droperidol dosing should be individualized and given in settings where vital signs and ECG can be monitored. The doses below are typical psychiatry-relevant ranges for adults and children in emergency or perioperative settings.

adult.agitation_im_initial: 5–10 mg IM as monotherapy or combined with a benzodiazepine; wait at least 10–30 minutes before adding more medication unless there is a clear safety emergency.
adult.agitation_iv_initial: 2.5–10 mg IV given slowly, as monotherapy or with a benzodiazepine; may repeat every 5 minutes until adequate sedation is reached, up to 20 mg total per episode.
adult.agitation_max_episode: Do not exceed 20 mg per episode for acute agitation; higher doses increase risk of QT prolongation, EPS, and hypotension.
adult.ponv_iv: 0.625–1.25 mg IV near the end of the procedure for postoperative nausea and vomiting prevention or rescue.
adult.manufacturer_initial: Labeling recommends a maximum initial dose of 2.5 mg IM/IV with cautious 1.25 mg increments, which is more conservative than many modern emergency department protocols.
adult.elderly: Start at the lowest end of the range (eg, 1.25–2.5 mg IV or 2.5–5 mg IM) with slower titration, given higher risk of hypotension, EPS, falls, and QT issues.
adult.hepatic: No formal numeric adjustment provided. Use lower starting doses and slower titration in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment with close monitoring.
adult.renal: No formal numeric adjustment provided. Use caution in moderate-to-severe renal impairment and monitor for prolonged effects.

pediatric.agitation_weight_based: Children ≥7 years and adolescents: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IM or IV (max 10 mg per dose) for acute agitation; data are limited and protocols vary.
pediatric.agitation_fixed_dosing: Children ≥7 years and adolescents: <34 kg: 0.625 mg; 34–57 kg: 1.25 mg; >57–68 kg: 1.875 mg; >68 kg: 2.5 mg IM or IV; may repeat in 15–30 minutes if still severely agitated.
pediatric.ponv_rescue: Children ≥2 years and adolescents: 0.01–0.075 mg/kg IM or IV (max 1.25 mg per dose) for rescue treatment of PONV; reserve for cases where other options have failed and use with extreme caution.
pediatric.special_caution: Avoid in children ≤2 years (per some international labeling) and use extreme caution in all pediatric patients due to increased risk of acute dystonic reactions and hyperprolactinemia.

sections.simple_explanation: For agitation, droperidol is usually dosed in the 5–10 mg range IM or 2.5–10 mg IV in adults, with repeat doses up to a 20 mg total for that episode. For nausea and vomiting, doses are much smaller—fractions of a milligram. In kids, dosing is usually based on weight. All of this happens in monitored settings, not at home.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Most people who receive droperidol are in the hospital already, often for surgery or a medical emergency. For special populations, the question is whether the short-term benefit outweighs the potential risks.
sections.pregnancy: Droperidol has been studied as an adjunct for severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, but current guidelines do not recommend it as a routine option. Short-term perioperative use may be considered if benefits outweigh risks, but alternatives are generally preferred. As with all antipsychotics, use in pregnancy should be individualized and reserved for situations where the mother’s safety is clearly at stake.
sections.lactation: It is not clear how much droperidol passes into breast milk. Some data suggest temporary effects on newborn behavior when used during cesarean delivery. A single perioperative dose is unlikely to cause serious problems in a healthy term infant, but caution is advised and monitoring for excess sleepiness, feeding problems, or poor tone is reasonable.
sections.pediatrics: Use cautiously and only when clearly indicated. Droperidol is considered a high-risk medication in children due to greater susceptibility to acute dystonic reactions and hyperprolactinemia. For agitation, data are limited and dosing should follow institutional protocols. For PONV, small weight-based doses may be used as rescue—not routine first-line.
sections.geriatrics: As with other antipsychotics, droperidol is on the Beers Criteria list of potentially inappropriate medications in older adults. Risks include stroke, cognitive decline, falls, SIADH/hyponatremia, and mortality in those with dementia. If used for severe agitation or antiemesis, start at very low doses, monitor closely, and reassess frequently.
sections.hepatic: Metabolized in the liver; use lower starting doses and titrate slowly in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment. Monitor for prolonged sedation and hypotension.
sections.renal: Renal impairment does not require a specific numeric adjustment, but accumulation of metabolites is possible. Use with caution and monitor for prolonged effects.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Baseline ECG before dosing to confirm QTc ≤440 ms in men or ≤450 ms in women.
Continuous ECG and cardiac monitoring for at least 2–3 hours after dosing, especially if higher or repeated doses are used.
Vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) before and after dosing, and more frequently in older or medically fragile patients.
Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium), renal function, and liver function as clinically indicated, especially if risk factors for QT prolongation are present.
Assessment for extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia, Parkinsonism) at baseline if on chronic dopamine blockers and after dosing; use a standardized EPS scale when possible.
Fall risk evaluation in older adults and those with orthostatic symptoms; provide assistance with ambulation.
Mental status and level of sedation: ensure that the patient is calm but still protecting their airway and breathing adequately.
Metabolic parameters (weight, fasting glucose, lipids) are less of a concern for single-dose use, but may still be relevant if droperidol is used repeatedly as an antipsychotic.
Prolactin-related symptoms (changes in menstruation, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction) if droperidol is used beyond a single exposure.
Documentation of indication, dosing, ECG findings, and any cardiac or neurologic adverse events for future risk/benefit discussions.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Droperidol is a parenteral-only medication—there is no pill, patch, or home version.
items: Injection solution (preservative-free): 2.5 mg/mL in 1 mL and 2 mL vials (generic).
Typically administered undiluted IM or as a slow IV push over 2–5 minutes in monitored settings.
No extended-release or oral formulations are available.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Droperidol is a butyrophenone antipsychotic that mainly blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the brain. Its antiemetic effect comes from blocking dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, the brain area that helps control nausea and vomiting. It also has alpha-adrenergic–blocking effects that cause blood vessels to relax, which can lower blood pressure. By calming overactive dopamine pathways, droperidol can quiet severe agitation, but the same dopamine blockade also explains its movement side effects (EPS) and, indirectly, some of its cardiac risk.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern practice, droperidol is a niche tool rather than a daily go-to medication. For psychiatry, it lives mostly in the emergency department and OR as part of rapid-tranquilization and perioperative nausea protocols. The black box warning for QT prolongation and torsades means it should be reserved for patients who do not respond adequately to safer options—like benzodiazepines, second-generation antipsychotics, or newer antiemetics—and only used with appropriate ECG monitoring. It is not a long-term maintenance medication for anxiety, mood, or psychotic disorders and is rarely, if ever, prescribed to take at home.

seo.title: Droperidol: Emergency Sedation, QT Risk, Dosing, and Side Effects
seo.description: Droperidol for acute agitation and postoperative nausea: fast-acting IM/IV antipsychotic/antiemetic with boxed warning for QT prolongation and torsades. Learn dosing ranges, onset, monitoring, and when it should—and should not—be used.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: Why would my team choose droperidol for agitation instead of something like lorazepam or haloperidol?
faqs.a: Droperidol is one of several injectable options for rapid tranquilization. Teams may choose it when a patient is extremely agitated, at risk of hurting themselves or others, and has not responded well to standard benzodiazepines or other antipsychotics. It often works quickly and can be combined with a benzodiazepine to balance calming with preserved breathing. Because of its heart-rhythm risks, it is typically reserved for monitored settings and used only when safer options are not enough.

faqs.q: How fast does droperidol work for agitation?
faqs.a: Droperidol usually starts working within 3–10 minutes after an IM or IV injection, with peak calming around 30 minutes. You may notice that you feel less driven to move, less angry, or less panicked relatively quickly. The main effects usually wear off over 2–4 hours, though some people feel groggy for longer.

faqs.q: What is the QT warning with droperidol, and should I be worried?
faqs.a: Droperidol can prolong the QT interval on your ECG. In rare cases this can trigger a dangerous rhythm called torsades de pointes, which can cause fainting or sudden cardiac arrest. To reduce this risk, clinicians check a baseline ECG, correct your potassium and magnesium if needed, and keep you on a heart monitor for 2–3 hours after dosing. Most patients receive droperidol safely, but this is a real risk—so we only use it when the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

faqs.q: Is droperidol a benzodiazepine or related to Xanax?
faqs.a: No. Droperidol is a first-generation antipsychotic in the butyrophenone family, more closely related to haloperidol than to benzodiazepines. It works mainly by blocking dopamine receptors rather than enhancing GABA. That means it does not create the same type of physical dependence benzodiazepines do, but it does bring its own risks like EPS and QT prolongation.

faqs.q: Can droperidol cause movement problems like dystonia or akathisia?
faqs.a: Yes. Because it blocks dopamine, droperidol can cause extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), especially at higher doses or in younger patients. Dystonia can look like painful neck twisting, eye rolling, or jaw stiffness. Akathisia feels like intense inner restlessness, like you have to keep moving. These reactions are treatable—usually with medications like diphenhydramine or benztropine—so tell staff immediately if you notice these symptoms.

faqs.q: Will I need to keep taking droperidol after I leave the hospital?
faqs.a: Almost never. Droperidol is mainly a one-time or short-term tool for a crisis—severe agitation or bad postoperative nausea. Once the episode has passed and the underlying issue is being addressed, there is typically no reason to continue droperidol as an outpatient medication.

faqs.q: Is droperidol safe in older adults?
faqs.a: Older adults are more sensitive to droperidol’s side effects, especially low blood pressure, confusion, falls, and heart-rhythm changes. Antipsychotics in general are on the Beers Criteria list of potentially inappropriate medications in people 65 and older. If droperidol is used, doses should be very low, monitoring should be tight, and the indication should be serious—such as dangerous agitation or refractory nausea in a monitored setting.

faqs.q: Can children receive droperidol for agitation or nausea?
faqs.a: Yes, but with a lot of caution. In pediatrics, droperidol is considered a high-risk medication due to higher rates of acute dystonic reactions and concerns about prolactin. When used, doses are carefully weight-based, and it is typically reserved for situations where other options have failed. Many centers avoid droperidol in very young children and use it only in monitored hospital settings.

faqs.q: What should I tell my care team before getting droperidol?
faqs.a: Let them know about any history of heart disease, fainting spells, seizures, long QT syndrome, electrolyte problems, or family history of sudden unexplained death. Also share your full medication list, especially diuretics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, or other QT-prolonging or sedating drugs. Finally, mention pregnancy or breastfeeding status so they can weigh risks and benefits.

faqs.q: Can droperidol be used for routine anxiety or insomnia?
faqs.a: No. Droperidol is not a routine treatment for chronic anxiety, panic, or insomnia. Its role is short-term and situation-specific, usually tied to surgery, procedures, or severe agitation. For ongoing anxiety or sleep problems, safer and better-studied options like therapy, SSRIs/SNRIs, non-sedating sleep strategies, or carefully chosen sleep medications are preferred.
